exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Point That Lies on a Transformed Curve

question.text: The point $(a,b)$ lies on the curve $y=e^x.$ Which of the following points must lie on $y = e^{2x}-3?$
question.explanation:
Method 1

To plot $y = e^{2x}-3,$ we apply the following steps:

  • First, we take the graph $y=e^x.$

  • Then, we stretch the graph by a scale factor of $\dfrac12$ parallel to the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=e^{2x}.$ After this transformation, the point $(a,b)$ will be mapped to the point \[ \left(\dfrac a2,b\right). \]

  • Finally, we shift the result vertically by $3$ units down and obtain the graph of $y = e^{2x}-3.$ After this transformation, the point $\left(\dfrac a2,b\right)$ will be mapped to the point \[ \left(\dfrac a2,b-3\right). \]

Method 2

Since the point $(a, b)$ lies on the graph of $y = e^x$, we have that $e^a = b.$

Now consider the graph of $y= e^{2x}-3.$ Substituting $x = \dfrac a 2$, we get

\begin{align*} y &= e^{2\cdot (a/2)}-3 \\[3pt] &= e^a -3 \\[3pt] &= b - 3. \end{align*}

Therefore, the point $\left(\dfrac a2,b-3\right)$ must lie on $y = e^{2x}-3.$

example.title: Finding a Point That Lies on a Transformed Curve

question.text: The point $(-1,1)$ lies on the curve $y = f(x).$ Which of the following points must lie on $y = 3f(x+2)?$
question.explanation:
Method 1

To plot $y = 3f(x+2),$ we apply the following steps:

  • First, we take the graph $y=f(x).$

  • Then, shift the graph horizontally by $2$ unit to the left and get the graph of $y=f(x+2).$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,1)$ will be mapped to the point
    \[ (-1-2,1) = (-3,1). \]

  • Finally, we stretch the result by a scale factor of $3$ parallel to the y-axis and get the graph of $y= 3f(x+2). $ After this transformation, the point $(-3,1)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (-3,3\cdot 1) = (-3,3). \]

Method 2

Since the point $(-1, 1)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x)$, we have that $f(-1) = 1.$

Now consider the graph of $y=3f(x+2).$ Substituting $x = -3$, we get

\begin{align*} y &=3 f(-3+2) \\[3pt] &= 3f(-1) \\[3pt] &= 3\cdot 1 \\[3pt] &= 3. \end{align*}

Therefore, the point $(-3,3)$ must lie on $y = 3f(x+2).$

exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Point That Lies on a Transformed Curve Given Another Transformed Curve

question.text: The point $(0, 3)$ lies on the curve $y = f(x-1).$ Which of the following points must lie on $y = f(x) + 2?$
question.explanation:
Method 1

We first find a point corresponding to $(0,3)$ on $y=f(x).$ Then, we find a corresponding point on $y=f(x)+2\mathbin{:}$

  • To plot the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following steps:

    • First, take the graph $y = f(x-1) .$

    • Then, we shift the graph horizontally $1$ unit to the left and get the graph of $y = f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(0,3)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (0-1,3)=(-1,3). \]

  • Next, to plot the graph of $y = f(x) + 2,$ we apply the following steps:

    • First, take the graph $y = f(x).$

    • Next, we shift the result vertically by $2$ units up and obtain the graph of $y = f(x) + 2.$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,3)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (-1,3+2)=(-1,5). \]

Method 2

Since the point $(0, 3)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x-1)$, we have that

\[ f(0-1) = 3 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f(-1)=3. \]

Now consider the graph of $y = f(x) + 2.$ Substituting $x = -1$, we get

\begin{align*} y &= f(-1) + 2 \\[3pt] &= 3 + 2 \\[3pt] &= 5. \end{align*}

Therefore, the point $(-1, 5)$ must lie on $y = f(x) + 2.$

example.title: Finding a Point That Lies on a Transformed Curve Given Another Transformed Curve

question.text: The point $(-2, -1)$ lies on the curve $y = f(x+1).$ Which of the following points must lie on $y = -f(x) + 5?$
question.explanation:
Method 1

We first find a point corresponding to $(-2,-1)$ on $y=f(x).$ Then, we find a corresponding point on $y=-f(x)+5\mathbin{:}$

  • To plot the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following steps:

    • First, take the graph $y = f(x+1).$

    • Then, we shift the graph horizontally $1$ unit to the right and get the graph of $y = f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(-2,-1)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (-2+1,-1)=(-1,-1). \]

  • Next, to plot the graph of $y = -f(x) + 5,$ we apply the following steps:

    • First, take the graph $y = f(x).$

    • Then, we reflect the result across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,-1)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (-1,-(-1)) = (-1,1). \]

    • Next, we shift the result vertically by $5$ units up and obtain the graph of $y = -f(x) + 5.$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,1)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (-1,1+5)=(-1,6). \]

Method 2

Since the point $(-2, -1)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x+1)$, we have that

\[ f(-2+1) = -1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f(-1)=-1. \]

Now consider the graph of $y = -f(x) + 5.$ Substituting $x = -1$, we get

\begin{align*} y &= -f(-1) + 5 \\[3pt] &= -(-1) + 5 \\[3pt] &= 6. \end{align*}

Therefore, the point $(-1, 6)$ must lie on $y = -f(x) + 5.$

question.text: The diagram above shows the global minimum and maximum of the function $y=f(x).$ What is the global minimum of $y=\dfrac{1}{2}f(x-5)?$
question.explanation:
Notice that the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{2}f(x-5)$ can be obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by

  • translating it by $5$ units to the right, and then

  • stretching it by a scale factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ parallel to the $y$-axis.

Since these transformations do not flip the graph across the $x$-axis, the combined transformation maps the global minimum of $y=f(x)$ to the global minimum of $y=\dfrac{1}{2}f(x-5).$ So, we need to find the image of $(-2,-4),$ the global minimum of $y=f(x),$ under the transformation.

To plot $y = \dfrac{1}{2}f(x-5),$ we apply the following steps:

  • First, we take the graph $y=f(x)$ that passes through $(-2,-4).$

  • Then, we shift the graph horizontally by $5$ units to the right and get the graph of $y=f(x-5).$ After this transformation, the point $(-2,-4)$ will be mapped to the point
    \[ (-2+5,-4) = (3,-4). \]

  • Finally, we stretch the result along the $y$-axis by a scale factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and get the graph of $y = \dfrac{1}{2}f(x-5).$ After this transformation, the point $(3,-4)$ will be mapped to the point \[ \left(3,\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot(-4)\right) = (3,-2). \]

Therefore, the global minimum of $y=\dfrac{1}{2}f(x-5)$ is $(3,-2).$

question.text: The diagram above shows the local minimum and maximum of the function $y=f(x).$ What is the local maximum of $y=f(x+3)-2?$
question.explanation:
Notice that the graph of $y=f(x+3)-2$ can be obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by

  • translating it by $3$ units to the left, and then

  • translating it by $2$ unit down.

Since these transformations do not flip the graph across the $x$-axis, the combined transformation maps the local maximum of $y=f(x)$ to the local maximum of $y=f(x+3)-2.$ So, we need to find the image of $(-2,6),$ the local maximum of $y=f(x),$ under the transformation.

To plot $y = f(x+3)-2,$ we apply the following steps:

  • First, we take the graph $y=f(x)$ that passes through $(-2,6).$

  • Then, we shift the graph horizontally by $3$ units to the left and get the graph of $y=f(x+3).$ After this transformation, the point $(-2,6)$ will be mapped to the point
    \[ (-2-3,6) = (-5,6). \]

  • Finally, we shift the result vertically by $2$ units downward and get the graph of $y = f(x+3)-2.$ After this transformation, the point $(-5,6)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (-5,6-2) = (-5,4). \]

Therefore, the local maximum of $y=f(x+3)-2$ is $(-5,4).$
